They play knight to f6 first, so that h4 comes next. The pawn bears down on d4, backing your d-pawn's push there, and f4, backing your f-pawn's push there. Their knight bears down on d5, backing their d-pawn's push there, and e4, holding back your e-pawn.
Got it — after your move, they play Bishop to d 6 if it's still legal.

Their bishop to d6 does two jobs: it stops your bishop takes c6, and it prepares castle kingside, to castle — a king left in the middle gets caught the moment the center opens. Their bishop develops to d6, joining the game. Your bishop to b5 goes after their knight on c6, the only piece guarding the pawn on e5.
Got it — after your move, they play Knight to a 5 if it's still legal.

They play knight to a5 first, so that c6 can hit your bishop on b5 — pieces behind a strong center reach either wing in a move or two. That was the move here — it develops into the game. Their knight bears down on c4, holding back your c-pawn. On a5 their knight touches only four squares; in the centre it would touch eight. A knight is worth the squares it reaches. A knight on the rim is dim.

Their a6 does two jobs: it stops your knight to b5, and it prepares b5. The bishop bears down on c4, backing your c-pawn's push there.

Nothing hinges on your next move — pick a sensible one and keep your clock for the hard decisions. c4 fights for the center from the flank: d5, keeping their knight off it. Their king is tucked safely away and the rook connects to the center. c4 is fine only because your bishop is already on e2 — with it back on b5, a-pawn takes b5 would cost you a bishop for a pawn.

Their pawn eyes the pawn on c4. The pawn bears down on e4, holding back their e-pawn. b3, c4 and d3 make a triangle: c4 is backed from both sides, so it can lead the expansion. Your king is still in the centre and the position is about to crack open — they already have a piece aimed down the e-file.
Got it — after your move, they play Pawn to c 5 if it's still legal.
c5 has a cost for them: no pawn of theirs can cover d5 again, and your knight on c2 is two moves from it; from there it would hit their knight on f6.

Their c5 fights for the center from the flank: d4, holding back your d-pawn. Their rook on e8 is tied down now: you hit the pawn on e5 twice and it is guarded twice — the rook is the guard that holds it. That is what pressure buys — a piece that cannot leave.
Got it — after your move, they play Bishop to c 7 if it's still legal.
Both kings on the kingside: no pawn race — pushing the pawns in front of your own king only weakens it, so the fight is in the centre and on the other wing.

Their bishop to c7 prepares d6. That was the move here — it castles your king into safety and swings the rook toward the center. How do you find a plan? First the forcing scan — checks, captures, threats. Then three things: where is their weakness, which of your pieces is worst, where is your pawn break? So the plan: break open with the pawn push that is ready now.
Got it — after your move, they play c takes b 4 if it's still legal.

Before your move, checks, captures, threats: nothing of yours could be taken, and nothing of theirs was free. Their weakness was the hole on d5 that no pawn of theirs can guard. Your worst piece was the bishop on e2. You found it — b4 was the pawn break that was ready.
That is the move this position asks for — it forks the knight on a5 and the pawn on c5.
Got it — after your move, they play Bishop to b 7 if it's still legal.

They play bishop to b7 first, so that rook to c8 can take the half-open c-file. You found it — it takes back the pawn. Their bishop takes aim along the long diagonal. Their a6 pawn is the key pawn: it guards b5, and if a6 drops, b5 goes with it.
Got it — after your move, they play Pawn to d 5 if it's still legal.
d5 has a cost for them: no pawn of theirs can cover c5 again, and your knight on b4 is two moves from it; from there it would hit their bishop on b7.

Their d5 stakes a claim in the center and opens lines for the pieces. Rook to c1 guards the pawn on c4, which their knight attacks. Their knight on f6 sits in front of their own f7 pawn, so while it stays there no pawn can come up to back up e5 — and you are already hitting e5.
Got it — after your move, they play Knight to c 6 if it's still legal.

Their knight trains on the knight on b4 — pressure they have to answer. c5 prepares c6, which would kick their bishop off b7. Your bishop on e2 looks dead for now — it is your own pawns that shut it in, and moving them brings it to life. Your c5 pushes your passed pawn — passed pawns must be pushed. Run the question now — what are they threatening? They're after your knight on b4. Deal with that before your own plan.
Got it — after your move, they play Pawn to a 5 if it's still legal.
Threat met. a3 keeps your knight on b4 safe.

Watch out — this costs a piece if you ignore it: their pawn on a5 hits your knight on b4, and a guard does not help: the pawn is worth less than your knight. A-pawn takes b4 wins your knight for their pawn, even after you take back.
That move does the job here — it guards the knight on b4, which they were about to win. Their a5 kicks your knight off b4, gaining time.
